Operates at least one public information or service website

situation.text: UK and EU public sector web teams operate under a legal requirement to obtain consent before setting non-essential cookies such as analytics cookies, and some teams' service-build workflows embed an Information Governance review of analytics plus a cookie-banner implementation step before a site goes live.

evidence.quote: You must have consent to set all other types of cookie.
Ensure Privacy Impact Assessment covers usage of analytics data
Add cookie banner to site, ensuring analytics respects user opt-in/opt-outs

situation.inference_basis: S7 states the UK legal consent requirement for non-essential cookies (tier 2 guidance); S6 shows a Scottish Government design-system workflow table (tier 2) that assigns a Privacy Impact Assessment check and a cookie-banner step specifically to analytics before a site launches. Combining these two distinct sources into one situation statement is an inference about how teams' build process relates to the consent requirement, not a single buyer's first-person account.; Publication date unknown; retrieval today does not establish current applicability.

incumbent_behaviour.text: GOV.UK's Government Digital Service runs Google Analytics, migrating its tracking from Universal Analytics to GA4, and queries the raw GA4 data directly in BigQuery and reports on it through Looker Studio.

evidence.quote: Google is replacing the current version of GA, Universal Analytics or UA, with a new version, GA4.
we’ve often had to rely on querying the raw GA4 data in BigQuery
We use it to build reports using our Google Analytics data.

incumbent_behaviour.inference_basis: Historical sources (2023-03-27); present applicability is not corroborated.

incumbent_behaviour.text: GOV.WALES runs Google Analytics alongside Plausible Analytics (described as aggregate-only with no personal data collected), self-hosted Matomo (described as cookieless), Crazy Egg page tagging, and a StackAdapt advertising pixel.

evidence.quote: We use Plausible Analytics on this site to collect some anonymous usage data for statistical purposes.
All the data is in aggregate only. No personal data is collected to Plausible.

To better understand site usage while respecting user privacy, we use Matomo Analytics, a self-hosted analytics solution. Matomo operates without setting cookies and utilises cookieless tracking to gather anonymous data on user behaviour.

Crazy Egg page tagging keeps a record of user clicks through our web site, identifying how often links are clicked and if users scroll on pages so that we may identify and make improvements where needed.

incumbent_behaviour.inference_basis: Publication date unknown; retrieval today does not establish current applicability.

incumbent_behaviour.text: gov.scot runs Google Analytics but anonymises the last three digits of visitor IP addresses, and presents a cookie banner offering 'Accept all cookies' or 'Use essential cookies only' choices.

evidence.quote: We use Google Analytics to collect information about how you use gov.scot.
We anonymise the last 3 digits of all gov.scot user IP addresses for Google Analytics, so that we can ensure that you are protected
Click 'Accept all cookies' to agree to all cookies that collect anonymous data. To only allow the cookies that make the site work, click 'Use essential cookies only.'

incumbent_behaviour.inference_basis: Publication date unknown; retrieval today does not establish current applicability.

incumbent_behaviour.text: Scottish Government Design System sites primarily use Google Tag Manager and Google Analytics, and the design system guidance also surfaces cookieless analytics tools for teams to consider as an alternative.

evidence.quote: Scottish Government Design System sites primarily use Google Tag Manager (GTM) and Google Analytics (GA).
Analytics tools which do not rely on cookies are also available and should be considered when deciding on an analytics solution

evidence.quote: Ensure Privacy Impact Assessment covers usage of analytics data

incumbent_behaviour.text: GDS makes its GA4 tracking schema and Data Protection Impact Assessment available to other UK government departments so they can reuse the schema or DPIA for their own GA4 implementations.

evidence.quote: to share our schema and Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) with other government departments.

We also hope departments may be able to learn from our approach and use our schema or our DPIA to support their own GA4 implementations. Increasing standardisation would create efficiencies across government, and hopefully save departments a lot of time and resource.

sophistication_basis.text: Public sector teams are already running specific named analytics products in production — Google Analytics alongside Plausible Analytics and self-hosted Matomo on gov.wales — rather than merely discussing analytics as a category, and Scottish Government design-system guidance explicitly names competing products (Simple Analytics, Fathom, Plausible) for teams to weigh against Google Analytics.

evidence.quote: we use Matomo Analytics, a self-hosted analytics solution
Analytics tools which do not rely on cookies are also available and should be considered when deciding on an analytics solution

sophistication_basis.inference_basis: Publication date unknown; retrieval today does not establish current applicability.

problems.statement: Teams that migrated GOV.UK's analytics from Universal Analytics to GA4 report that GA4's interface and data handling limit routine reporting: large volumes of event data get grouped into an unusable '(other)' category, strict API quota limits restrict additional reporting tools, multiple reporting views are no longer available (the comparable sub-properties cost more), and character limits with event batching disrupt plotting user journeys.

evidence.quote: data is currently grouped into one line and labelled (other)
hamper our ability to use additional tools for reporting and analysis.
Unlike in UA, you can’t have multiple reporting views in GA4 — sub-properties, the most comparable feature, cost more and do not have the same functionality.

Character limits on the data that we send to GA4 affect our ability to collect data. GA4 also groups events in batches when sending them, which causes issues plotting user journeys and comparing UA and GA4 data.

problems.cost: Daily GA4 data tables are described as almost 20% larger than under Universal Analytics, which the team expects to increase storage costs.

cost_evidence.quote: Changes to the data structure mean that our daily data tables are almost 20% larger in GA4, so we expect storage costs to increase.

review_notes: Historical sources (2023-03-27); present applicability is not corroborated.
Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.

triggers.text: A regulatory decision finding that Google Analytics cookies are not exempt from consent requirements can be a trigger for organisations to reassess their analytics vendor and cookie setup.

evidence.quote: la formation restreinte de la CNIL a relevé dans sa décision n° SAN-2020-008 du 18 novembre que les *«*cookies [Google Analytics] n’ont pas pour finalité exclusive de permettre ou de faciliter la communication par voie électronique et ne sont pas strictement nécessaires à la fourniture du service*»*.

triggers.inference_basis: S8 is CNIL (tier 3) guidance reporting a regulatory decision about Google Analytics cookies not qualifying for the measurement exemption; this is a third party's interpretation of the law, not a tier-1 buyer statement of being triggered, so presenting it as a cause of buyer action is an inference rather than a grounded buyer-reported trigger.; Publication date unknown; retrieval today does not establish current applicability.
